PostgreSQL 17 improves I/O by combining multiple 8KB page reads into a single system call using preadv. So, Even though preadv() existed since PostgreSQL 14 (for WAL and internal uses), data reads were still always 8KB per syscall. Starting in PostgreSQL 17, full support for preadv() and pwritev() was added for combined I/O — enabling multi-page reads and writes. content.text:
Here are the main index-related changes in PostgreSQL 17 (released Sept 2024):

The biggest one is an improvement to **B-tree scans with multiple values in an `IN` clause** (or `= ANY(...)`). Previously, a query like `WHERE id IN (1, 5, 9, 20)` would do a separate index descent for each value. PG17 can now handle the whole set in a single index scan, which cuts I/O substantially on those queries.

Second, **BRIN indexes can now be built in parallel**. BRIN indexes are used on very large, naturally-ordered tables (think time-series data ordered by timestamp). In PG16 the build was single-threaded; PG17 parallelizes it, so creation is much faster.

Third, a planner improvement around **`IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`**: the optimizer now recognizes when a column is declared `NOT NULL` and can skip scans that would return nothing (e.g. an `IS NULL` check on a NOT NULL column). Not strictly an index feature, but it affects whether and how indexes get scanned.

The first one is the most impactful for everyday query tuning — lots of real queries filter on a list of IDs.

Want me to go deeper on any of these? The multi-value B-tree scan in particular has some nuance about when the planner actually chooses it.

key_takeaways: PostgreSQL 17 improves B-tree scans for queries with multiple values in an IN clause (or = ANY(...)): instead of a separate index descent per value, the whole set is handled in a single index scan, reducing I/O — this was framed as the most impactful change for everyday query tuning.
BRIN indexes can now be built in parallel in PG17 (previously single-threaded in PG16), making index creation much faster on very large, naturally-ordered tables like time-series data.
A planner improvement lets the optimizer recognize NOT NULL columns and skip scans that would return nothing for IS NULL / IS NOT NULL checks, which affects whether and how indexes get scanned.
